## Meta-review synthesis

What the loop converged on. Across three rounds of generation, review, tournament, and evolution, the candidate space organized itself into six mechanistic families, and the tournament's top of table is dominated by two of them: direct androgen-axis blockade (H001/H014 at Elo 1548) and a cluster of mechanistically orthogonal topical agents at 1532/1516 (calcipotriene, the iron chelators, dutasteride, and a band of vasodilator/anti-inflammatory drugs). The loop's evolution stage did real work: the two redundant AR-antagonist lineages were merged into one program (H014 carries clascoterone as lead with bicalutamide demoted to in-vitro benchmark), the deferiprone hypothesis deleted its own confounded HIF/PHD arm after review, and the calcipotriene and lovastatin hypotheses absorbed their reviewers' strongest objections as explicit falsification gates rather than rebutting them in prose. Where the loop is confident: the androgen axis is the best-validated target class (OpenTargets disease-association scores of 0.44 for AR and 0.70 for SRD5A2 confirm the drug-target/disease-target overlap), and human hypertrichosis side-effect data ground the KATP, calcineurin, and prostaglandin axes. Where it is guessing: every non-androgen mechanism rests on in-vitro or organ-culture extrapolation with zero human AGA efficacy data, and the oxidative-stress, microinflammation, and VDR arms are plausible-adjacent rather than validated.

How validation reshaped the ranking. Elo alone would put dutasteride (H025) and calcipotriene (H017) in the top five, but external data discount both: dutasteride has 10 prior AGA trials, 280 PubMed co-mentions, and novelty score 0.004 — it is effectively standard of care, not a repurposing finding, and the same applies to finasteride (1084 co-mentions), spironolactone (214), and cyclosporine (283), which despite Elos of 1500-1531 are excluded from the picks on novelty grounds. Calcipotriene already has 5 alopecia trials including a female-pattern-hair-loss study, shows no OpenTargets VDR-AGA overlap, and its own final form concedes the mechanism may be ligand-independent — a severe unresolved caveat. Conversely, clascoterone (H014) keeps the top slot despite 3 completed trials (up to phase 3, SCALP2) because its own hypothesis honestly reframes the value proposition: not discovery novelty but the fastest, lowest-risk execution of receptor-level AR blockade, with the strongest confidence rating (4) in the run and the AR disease-gene overlap; its crowdedness is a de-risking feature for proof-of-mechanism, not a reason to discard it, and it subsumes H001's stronger-affinity chemistry as backup. Diazoxide (H027) is promoted well above its Elo rank (11th): zero prior AGA trials, a KCNJ11 disease-gene overlap (0.41), and a crisp answer to the field's largest unmet need — minoxidil's SULT1A1-dependent non-responder fraction. Deferiprone (H026) is kept over its Elo-tied sibling deferoxamine (H021) because it solves the skin-penetration problem that makes DFO's topical route infeasible; both have zero prior trials and top-tier novelty (0.14-0.20), so the deliverable molecule wins. Roflumilast (H030) has the joint-highest novelty score (0.25), only one prior trial (alopecia areata, not AGA), two dossier-anchored mechanisms, and an already-approved scalp foam that removes the delivery objection outright. Misoprostol (H005) is included from mid-table (Elo 1484) as the high-risk/high-novelty slot: zero trials, novelty 0.14, and it attacks a human-validated prostaglandin pathway from a direction no prior program has tried.

Limitations and discriminating experiments. This is prioritization, not proof: the Elo spread from rank 1 to rank 13 is only ~48 points, so orderings within the top band are soft, and 12 of 32 hypotheses received no external validation at all. The most efficient discriminating experiments, in order: (1) the scalp maximal-use pharmacokinetic study already built into H014 as its gating deliverable — it converts the whole AR-antagonist family from asserted safety to measured safety; (2) a head-to-head human follicle organ-culture panel of H027 versus minoxidil across SULT1A1-genotyped donors, which directly tests the responder-variability claim that is diazoxide's entire reason to exist; (3) H026's pre-registered epithelial-versus-papilla competition assay with its termination rule — a cheap kill-switch experiment for the oxidative-stress theme; (4) cAMP and perifollicular-inflammation readouts for H030 in the same organ-culture system, separating its two claimed mechanisms; and (5) EP-receptor engagement plus anagen-maintenance readout for H005 versus a latanoprost positive control, which would validate or kill the E-series prostaglandin direction in one experiment. Running these five readouts in a shared organ-culture platform would, within one experimental cycle, either collapse the six themes to the one or two that survive contact with human follicle tissue or hand the program a genuinely diversified portfolio.

**Themes:** Direct androgen-axis blockade: topical receptor-level AR antagonists (bicalutamide H001, clascoterone H014, spironolactone H010) and 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors (dutasteride H025, finasteride H011) — the most mechanistically validated axis in AGA, and also the most crowded.; Perifollicular microcirculation and vasodilation: KATP-channel openers (diazoxide H027 as a non-prodrug successor to minoxidil) and phosphodiesterase inhibitors (pentoxifylline H008, tadalafil H016, cilostazol H019) targeting the perfusion niche of miniaturizing follicles.; Perifollicular microinflammation and immunomodulation: calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus H028, cyclosporine H012), selective PDE4 inhibition (roflumilast H030), JAK inhibition (tofacitinib H013), and the mevalonate/anti-inflammatory arm of topical statins (lovastatin H009).; Iron chelation and oxidative-stress control in balding dermal papilla: deferoxamine H021 (HIF-1alpha/angiogenic arm) and deferiprone H026 (redox-iron/Fenton arm with skin-permeable chemistry).; Prostaglandin balance modulation: misoprostol H005 as direct E-series EP agonism, attacking the PGD2-elevated balding-scalp environment from the opposite side of prior F2alpha-analog and DP2-antagonist efforts.; Hair-cycle, stem-cell niche, and senescence signaling: VDR agonism (calcipotriene H017), mTORC1/senescence modulation (sirolimus H004), and ion-channel or epigenetic cycle modulators (ezogabine H018, phenytoin H029, valproic acid H002).

**Top picks:** H014, H027, H026, H030, H005

## Candidate details

### 1. BICALUTAMIDE (H001)

- ChEMBL: CHEMBL409 | Elo 1548 | confidence 3/5 | route: topical | origin: generation (round 1)
- **Mechanism:** Bicalutamide is a pure non-steroidal androgen receptor (AR) antagonist that competitively occupies the AR ligand-binding pocket and blocks AR dimerization and nuclear translocation. Per the dossier (section 1), DHT-driven AR signaling in dermal papilla cells is the initiating event of follicle miniaturization in AGA, and the excerpt literature confirms that preventing AR activation/nuclear translocation rescues dermal papilla cells from DHT-induced apoptosis, senescence, and hair-cycle arrest. Topically delivered bicalutamide could block AR locally in dermal papilla cells at the receptor level, downstream of 5-alpha-reductase, catching DHT from both type I and type II isoenzymes.
- **Evidence:** PMID 39306884 demonstrates that competitive AR binding preventing AR dimerization/nuclear translocation alleviates DHT-induced dermal papilla cell damage and reverses androgenetic alopecia in a DHT-induced mouse model, directly validating receptor-level blockade as a therapeutic strategy. PMID 24244503 shows AR signaling drives premature senescence of dermal papilla cells specifically in balding-prone scalp regions, and AR knockdown abolishes the effect — supporting local AR antagonism as disease-modifying. (refs: PMID 39306884, PMID 24244503)
- **Safety:** Oral bicalutamide causes gynecomastia, breast tenderness, and hepatotoxicity — unacceptable systemically for a cosmetic indication. Topical formulation at low concentration with minimal systemic absorption is essential; percutaneous absorption must be characterized. Best suited initially for male pattern AGA where oral anti-androgens are intolerable; avoid in pregnancy-exposed partners. Local skin irritation is the main expected topical risk.
- **Novelty rationale:** Systemic AR antagonists are unusable in men due to feminizing side effects, which is why receptor-level blockade is absent from male AGA therapy despite being the most direct mechanism. A topically restricted bicalutamide formulation for male AGA is a genuinely new angle — fluridil attempted this niche but is a weaker, less-characterized antagonist and is not widely approved.

Reviews:
- plausibility 8/10, evidence 6/10, safety 6/10, novelty 7/10 — verdict **accept**. Mechanistically the tightest proposal in the set: it sits directly on the therapeutically validated DHT-AR axis and blocks downstream of both 5-alpha-reductase isoforms. But the headline evidence is misattributed by proxy — PMID 39306884 is about obacunone, a citrus limonoid, not bicalutamide; it validates receptor-level AR blockade as a strategy, yet says nothing about this drug. No cited evidence shows bicalutamide itself affects dermal papilla cells or hair. Two further gaps: (1) bicalutamide (MW ~430) has essentially no characterized percutaneous absorption profile, so the central safety claim (topically confined, non-feminizing in men) is asserted, not demonstrated — even low systemic levels of a pure anti-androgen in men could cause gynecomastia, and hepatotoxicity is a class label; (2) the novelty claim is overstated, as topical anti-androgens (fluridil, and bicalutamide itself has appeared in topical-hair patents/early studies) mean this niche is not untouched. Proceed, but only with a required percutaneous-absorption/systemic-exposure package and a direct in-vitro dermal papilla experiment before any efficacy claims.

### 2. clascoterone (cortexolone 17alpha-propionate) (H014)

- ChEMBL: CHEMBL3590187 | Elo 1548 | confidence 4/5 | route: topical | origin: evolution (round 1)
- **Mechanism:** Clascoterone is a topical androgen receptor (AR) antagonist, FDA-approved for acne, that competitively inhibits DHT binding at the AR in human dermal papilla cells and is rapidly hydrolyzed to the much less active cortexolone, giving it an intrinsically low systemic anti-androgenic footprint. DHT-driven AR signaling in dermal papilla cells is the initiating, therapeutically validated event of follicle miniaturization in AGA (dossier section 1; finasteride/dutasteride precedent), and receptor-level blockade acts downstream of both 5-alpha-reductase isoforms, catching DHT from type I and type II enzyme activity alike. Final form of the claim: this is not a repurposing discovery but the fastest, lowest-risk legitimate vehicle for the first human proof-of-mechanism readout of receptor-level AR blockade in AGA. The bicalutamide lineage (parent H001) is folded in rather than carried separately: bicalutamide's critique - no drug-specific follicle evidence and an uncharacterized percutaneous absorption profile for a pure, non-feminizing-in-men claim - is resolved by demoting bicalutamide to a benchmark comparator in the program's first in-vitro step (head-to-head AR occupancy and DHT-antagonism in human dermal papilla cells versus clascoterone), so the stronger-affinity molecule remains available as backup chemistry only if its own absorption package is later generated, while the approved, characterized topical package of clascoterone carries the program.
- **Evidence:** PMID 30811143 is the drug-specific anchor: clascoterone antagonizes AR in human dermal papilla cells in vitro, and its abstract references the ongoing phase 2 scalp program, which is why no discovery novelty is claimed. PMID 39306884 (the obacunone paper) is retained strictly as strategy-level support: receptor-level AR blockade preventing dimerization/nuclear translocation rescues dermal papilla cells in a DHT-induced mouse model - it says nothing about clascoterone or bicalutamide and is cited only for the class. PMID 24244503 shows AR signaling drives premature senescence of balding dermal papilla cells and that AR knockdown abolishes it. No cited source contains human scalp efficacy data for any topical AR antagonist; that remains the program's central open question, to be answered by the phase 2 readout rather than asserted. (refs: PMID 30811143, PMID 39306884, PMID 24244503)
- **Safety:** Approved-label topical clascoterone has low systemic exposure because absorbed drug is hydrolyzed to cortexolone, with no clinically meaningful HPA-axis effect at acne doses. The standing weakest link is adopted as the gating study: scalp surface area far exceeds facial acne treatment areas, so the program opens with a maximal-use scalp pharmacokinetic study quantifying serum clascoterone and cortexolone after full-scalp cosmetic dosing before any efficacy interpretation. Avoid use in pregnancy and in women trying to conceive until reproductive safety margins are quantified. Local irritation is the main expected topical risk. This directly discharges the H001 critique that a topically-confined, non-feminizing profile was asserted rather than demonstrated: here it is the measured first deliverable, for a drug whose hydrolysis-based deactivation makes the favorable outcome plausible.
- **Novelty rationale:** What materially changed in this final form: (1) the two top-ranked AR-antagonist lineages are merged into one program instead of competing as redundant monotherapies - clascoterone is the lead (approved topical package, drug-specific dermal papilla data) and bicalutamide survives only as an in-vitro benchmark and conditional backup, which resolves H001's misattributed-evidence and uncharacterized-absorption critiques by construction; (2) the novelty claim is set at its final honest level - accelerate and de-risk an already-public AGA program (phase 2 trials referenced in PMID 30811143), with the contribution being a scalp-PK-first development sequence and clean separation of strategy-level from drug-specific evidence, not a new mechanism; (3) the absence of human scalp efficacy data is the stated gating readout, not a gap to be argued around. No claim of novel science survives; the value is execution speed on the most validated axis in AGA.

Reviews:
- plausibility 8/10, evidence 7/10, safety 9/10, novelty 5/10 — verdict **accept**. The strongest of the batch, but two honest caveats keep it from a clean bill. First, the novelty claim must be narrowed further than the authors already did: clascoterone is not merely 'not an established hair treatment' — it is an ACTIVE, publicly known AGA development program (phase 2 scalp trials are referenced in the very abstract of PMID 30811143), so the proposal is closer to 'accelerate an existing program' than to a repurposing discovery; scoring it as novel science would overstate it. Second, the in vitro dermal papilla antagonism (PMID 30811143, verified: correctly attributed to clascoterone) plus acne-approval safety package do not by themselves demonstrate scalp efficacy — androgen axis validation by finasteride analogy is supportive but receptor-level blockade still lacks published human AGA efficacy data in the cited set. The handling of PMID 39306884 is exemplary: it is indeed the obacunone paper, and the authors explicitly downgrade it to strategy-level support rather than laundering it into drug-specific evidence. PMID 24244503 (AR-driven premature senescence of dermal papilla cells) is correctly attributed. PMID verification: all three source_refs exist in the corpus and match their stated content. Weakest link: scalp surface-area systemic exposure and the absence of cited human scalp efficacy data, not the mechanism.

### 3. calcipotriene (H017)

- ChEMBL: CHEMBL1200666 | Elo 1532 | confidence 2/5 | route: topical | origin: generation (round 2)
- **Mechanism:** Calcipotriene is a topical vitamin D receptor (VDR) agonist with decades of dermatologic safety experience. The hypothesis remains explicitly conditional and now carries its falsification gate in fully specified form: topical calcipotriene promotes anagen re-entry in miniaturizing follicles ONLY IF human follicle VDR retains a ligand-dependent signaling component relevant to hair cycling. The defining experiment: organ-cultured human scalp follicles in four arms - VDR knockdown, VDR knockdown plus calcipotriene rescue, calcipotriene alone, vehicle - with anagen entry and hair follicle stem cell activation as readouts. Because the established hair-cycling role of VDR comes largely from loss-of-function genetics with a substantial ligand-INDEPENDENT (unliganded scaffold) component, a calcipotriene rescue of the knockdown phenotype is the only outcome that licenses proceeding; failure of rescue, or absence of a calcipotriene-alone effect, terminates the hypothesis. If a ligand-dependent arm exists, calcipotriene acts downstream of and orthogonally to the androgen axis, positioning it strictly as an adjunct to AR-directed therapy.
- **Evidence:** PMID 40110814, a general AGA pathogenesis review, remains the only cited source and only for what it supports: AGA involves follicle miniaturization and stem-cell/niche dysfunction, and current drugs are inadequate. The standing corrections are retained verbatim: nothing cited connects calcipotriene or VDR agonism to anagen promotion in follicles, and topical calcipotriene has already been tried in alopecia areata with mixed/weak results. The reviewer's remaining ask - direct VDR/hair-cycling literature - is answered honestly within the cited corpus: it does not exist here, which is itself the reason the ligand-dependence experiment, not a literature claim, carries the mechanism. No efficacy is asserted in advance of that experiment. (refs: PMID 40110814)
- **Safety:** The best topical safety profile in this hypothesis set, as the reviewer acknowledged: decades of psoriasis use. Risks are local irritation and, over large body surface areas, hypercalcemia - bounded at scalp-limited cosmetic doses by a maximum weekly dose in any study. No systemic endocrine or anti-androgenic effects at intended exposure, so it is suitable for both men and women, including women of childbearing potential - a genuine differentiator from every AR-axis proposal in this set.
- **Novelty rationale:** What materially changed in final form: the ligand-dependence gate is upgraded from a described experiment to a fully specified four-arm design with named readouts and an explicit termination rule, so the reviewer's central trap (a VDR agonist cannot phenocopy a ligand-independent VDR function) is now the hypothesis's first measurable output rather than an objection answered in prose. The novelty claim stays at its narrowed level: VDR agonism untested in AGA specifically, contingent on demonstrated ligand-dependent hair-cycling function, with alopecia areata precedent conceded. Confidence stays low by design - the premise may not survive its own gate.

Reviews:
- plausibility 4/10, evidence 2/10, safety 8/10, novelty 7/10 — verdict **revise**. The idea is genuinely underexplored and the safety profile is the best topical one in this batch, but the mechanism has a known scientific trap the authors did not address: the hair-follicle-cycling function of VDR is established largely through VDR LOSS-OF-FUNCTION genetics, and a substantial literature indicates VDR's role in hair cycling is at least partly LIGAND-INDEPENDENT — i.e., unliganded VDR acting as a transcriptional/scaffold factor in keratinocytes. If the alopecia of VDR disruption reflects ligand-independent functions, then a VDR AGONIST like calcipotriene does not phenocopy VDR's hair-promoting role and the central mechanistic premise collapses. The proposal must engage this directly with ligand-dependent evidence in follicle models before it is credible. Evidence as cited is nearly empty: PMID 40110814 (verified: general AGA pathogenesis review) is the only source, and leaning on it for the specific claim that hair follicle stem cell loss is an AGA driver is a thin read of a broad review; nothing cited connects calcipotriene or VDR agonism to anagen promotion in follicles. Also note topical calcipotriene has already been tried (with mixed/weak results) in alopecia areata, which partially undercuts the 'never pursued' framing. Revise by: citing direct VDR/hair-cycling literature, resolving the ligand-dependence question, and adding preclinical follicle data.

### 4. DEFEROXAMINE (H021)

- ChEMBL: CHEMBL556 | Elo 1532 | confidence 2/5 | route: topical | origin: generation (round 2)
- **Mechanism:** Deferoxamine is an iron chelator that, applied topically, stabilizes HIF-1alpha by chelating the iron cofactor of prolyl hydroxylases, driving a local pro-angiogenic VEGF program. Miniaturized AGA follicles lose their supporting microvasculature as they shrink; restoring perifollicular angiogenic signaling could support re-enlargement. Additionally, iron chelation removes the Fenton-reaction substrate, reducing hydroxyl-radical generation - directly relevant to the oxidative stress and androgen-driven DNA damage reported in balding dermal papilla cells.
- **Evidence:** PMID 24244503 demonstrates DNA damage (gamma-H2AX foci) and premature senescence in androgen-exposed balding dermal papilla cells, a phenotype oxidative stress contributes to. PMID 40110814 lists oxidative-stress-state changes among AGA pathogenic factors. The dossier (section 8) describes ROS and senescence in balding papilla. No excerpt tests deferoxamine on follicles; the angiogenesis rationale comes from its known HIF pharmacology in wound-healing contexts. (refs: PMID 24244503, PMID 40110814)
- **Safety:** Systemic deferoxamine (infusion) carries hypotension, and auditory/ocular toxicity with chronic use - irrelevant at topical cosmetic exposure. Topical deferoxamine has been used experimentally on wounds with acceptable tolerability; it is hydrophilic, so penetration enhancement would be needed. Local irritation is the main expected risk.
- **Novelty rationale:** Pharmacologic HIF-1alpha stabilization to rebuild the perifollicular vascular niche is a mechanism absent from the entire round-1 set and from AGA practice; the same molecule secondarily addresses oxidative DNA damage, a documented balding-papilla phenotype, making it a two-pronged but single-drug proposal.

Reviews:
- plausibility 6/10, evidence 5/10, safety 7/10, novelty 8/10 — verdict **revise**. The strongest of this set, but with two adversarial points. First, delivery: deferoxamine is a highly hydrophilic ~560 Da iron chelator with notoriously poor passive skin penetration; the proposal waves at 'penetration enhancement' without acknowledging that achieving follicular concentrations sufficient to chelate prolyl-hydroxylase iron in dermal papilla is the make-or-break experiment, and no data are offered. Second, an unexamined mechanism contradiction: iron chelation is antiproliferative - deferoxamine starves ribonucleotide reductase and arrests cycling cells, which is why it has been explored as an anticancer agent. The anagen follicle epithelium is among the most proliferative tissue in the body, so the same drug that stabilizes HIF-1alpha and blunts Fenton chemistry could simultaneously brake the epithelial proliferation needed for re-enlargement; the dose window between pro-angiogenic and antiproliferative is unmapped. The cited evidence checks out (PMID 24244503 verified - androgen/AR-driven premature senescence with gamma-H2AX in dermal papilla; PMID 40110814 verified - oxidative stress state listed among AGA factors), and the wound-healing HIF pharmacology is real but transplant-naive. Topical route keeps systemic toxicity irrelevant. Proceed only after penetration and follicle-cell proliferation readouts.

- Novelty: 6 PubMed hair co-mentions (novelty score 0.143)

### 5. deferiprone (H026)

- ChEMBL: CHEMBL70927 | Elo 1532 | confidence 2/5 | route: topical | origin: evolution (round 2)
- **Mechanism:** Deferiprone is an approved oral iron chelator that is small (~139 Da) and moderately lipophilic, giving it the passive skin permeability that made-or-break delivery of its hydrophilic parent deferoxamine impossible. In final form the mechanism is narrowed to a single, uncontaminated arm: local chelation of redox-active iron in balding dermal papilla to remove the Fenton-reaction substrate, reducing hydroxyl-radical generation and the androgen-driven oxidative DNA damage documented in balding papilla cells. The HIF-1alpha/prolyl-hydroxylase arm is dropped entirely, because deferiprone is itself a 2-oxoglutarate oxygenase inhibitor and any HIF/PHD readout is uninterpretable - the reviewer's confounder point is resolved by eliminating the confounded readout rather than qualifying it. The antiproliferative contradiction is resolved by redesigning the gate so it no longer presupposes a therapeutic window exists: a head-to-head, same-follicle dose-response comparing dermal papilla oxidative-rescue (gamma-H2AX, 8-oxo-dG) against epithelial matrix proliferation (Ki-67) across topically achievable concentrations, with a pre-declared kill criterion - if epithelial proliferation is suppressed at every concentration that rescues papilla oxidative damage, the hypothesis terminates, conceding the reviewer's point that the epithelium's higher iron demand may leave no window.
- **Evidence:** Both citations are retained at their verified scope: PMID 24244503 demonstrates DNA damage (gamma-H2AX foci) and premature senescence in androgen-exposed balding dermal papilla cells, a phenotype oxidative stress contributes to; PMID 40110814 lists oxidative-stress-state changes among AGA pathogenic factors. It is stated plainly, as the reviewer required, that the follicle evidence base for any iron chelator is zero - no efficacy is asserted, and the redesigned organ-culture titration (run first and cheaply, per the review) is the hypothesis's entire first milestone. (refs: PMID 24244503, PMID 40110814)
- **Safety:** Deferiprone's systemic liabilities (agranulocytosis with chronic oral dosing, requiring weekly neutrophil monitoring) are the reason for topical-only positioning; because the molecule is readily absorbed, systemic uptake is quantified in a first PK step before any repeat-dose human exposure. The dominant local safety question - antiproliferative injury to anagen epithelium via ribonucleotide reductase iron starvation - is answered by the built-in same-follicle proliferation readout before any human application. Local irritation and chelator-related trace-metal imbalance in skin are the other expected topical risks.
- **Novelty rationale:** What materially changed in final form: (1) the PHD/HIF arm is deleted outright, removing the off-target 2-oxoglutarate-oxygenase confounder the reviewer identified instead of merely acknowledging it; (2) the gating experiment is restructured from a window-search (which presupposed the answer) into an unbiased epithelial-versus-papilla competition with a pre-declared termination rule, so the hypothesis can now falsify itself on the reviewer's exact objection; (3) the mechanism is reduced to the single arm anchored in verified balding-papilla phenotype evidence. Iron chelation for balding-papilla oxidative damage remains absent from AGA practice and from every other hypothesis in this set.

Reviews:
- plausibility 5/10, evidence 3/10, safety 5/10, novelty 7/10 — verdict **revise**. The drug swap from deferoxamine to deferiprone genuinely fixes the delivery objection, and citing scope is honest (PMID 24244503 is accurately described as showing gamma-H2AX/premature senescence in androgen-exposed balding dermal papilla cells; PMID 40110814 is a general pathogenesis review). But the weakest link is the same one the parent died on, merely relabeled: iron chelation starves ribonucleotide reductase in exactly the most proliferative compartment of the follicle, the anagen matrix. The hypothesis's own gating experiment presupposes a 'pro-papilla antioxidant window below the antiproliferative threshold' exists — there is no a priori reason to believe one does, since the epithelium's iron demand is far higher than the papilla's. A secondary confounder: deferiprone is itself a 2-oxoglutarate oxygenase inhibitor, so any HIF/prolyl-hydroxylase readout will be contaminated by off-target PHD inhibition. Evidence base for iron chelation in follicles is zero. Proceed only if the organ-culture titration is run first and cheaply; the honest framing saves it from reject.

### 6. dutasteride (H025)

- ChEMBL: CHEMBL1200969 | Elo 1531 | confidence 3/5 | route: topical (microneedling-assisted) | origin: generation (round 2)
- **Mechanism:** Dutasteride is a dual type I/II 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor and an established, efficacious AGA drug; this is a delivery/pharmacokinetic hypothesis, not a new molecular claim. The two parent delivery proposals are merged into one decisive study question: does microneedling-assisted topical dutasteride achieve high follicular 5-alpha-reductase suppression - including the type I isoform oral finasteride misses - at lower serum DHT suppression than oral dosing? The H011 critiques are resolved structurally: the minoxidil confound is removed by excluding minoxidil from the design entirely (nothing is attributed to the combination trial), and the self-defeating safety logic (microneedling disrupts the stratum corneum and increases systemic absorption) is converted from an embarrassment into the primary measurement - the hypothesis predicts a follicular-to-systemic exposure gradient and lives or dies on measuring it. Dutasteride is retained over finasteride for maximal local dual-isoform blockade, the strongest version of the validated androgen-axis target (dossier section 1).
- **Evidence:** The corrected characterization of PMID 39954111 is retained verbatim: it is a 45-patient trial (15 per arm) in which microneedling plus minoxidil plus finasteride was NOT significantly better than minoxidil plus finasteride alone on hair density or shaft diameter (P>0.05 for both), with significance only against minoxidil monotherapy and on Norwood-Hamilton grade/self-rating - it is weak adjunct support and, per the H011 review, its microneedling signal is equally consistent with wound-healing growth stimulation, so it is cited only as rationale that scalp microneedling is tolerated and testable, not as delivery evidence. PMID 40110814 supports abnormal follicular 5-alpha-reductase elevation as pathogenic. The actual load-bearing facts - dutasteride's established oral AGA efficacy and topical/intradermal dutasteride precedent - sit outside the cited set and are used only to justify why the PK question is worth answering. The hypothesis's evidence claim is confined to its planned measurements: follicular drug levels, scalp 5AR activity, and serum DHT under microneedle-assisted topical dosing versus oral dosing. (refs: PMID 39954111, PMID 40110814)
- **Safety:** Oral dutasteride carries sexual side effects, gynecomastia, an approximately 5-week half-life, and teratogenic risk to a male fetus. Because microneedling deliberately increases skin permeability, serum DHT is the primary safety endpoint of the proposed study rather than an assumption of safety: if systemic DHT suppression under microneedle-assisted topical dosing approaches oral levels, the hypothesis fails on its own terms. The long-half-life burden is now explicit - any meaningful absorbed dose produces weeks of persistent systemic DHT suppression after cessation - and the formulation itself requires pregnant-partner handling precautions. Microneedling adds transient erythema and infection risk, mitigated by sterile single-use cartridges and standardized depth.
- **Novelty rationale:** What materially changed in this final merge: (1) the finasteride (H011) and dutasteride (H025) delivery proposals are unified into a single falsifiable PK/PD question with a concrete measurement plan - follicular 5AR inhibition versus serum DHT suppression, topical-plus-microneedling versus oral - which is exactly the honest reframing the H011 reviewer demanded; (2) the minoxidil confound is eliminated by design rather than by argument; (3) the novelty claim is set at its corrected level: topical finasteride is already EU-approved, intradermal and topical dutasteride have already been studied, and microneedling-plus-drug protocols are widespread, so this is incremental delivery optimization of an established drug whose residual value is finasteride-level-or-better local efficacy (via type I coverage) at lower systemic exposure - to be proven or refuted by the PK data, not presumed.

Reviews:
- plausibility 7/10, evidence 4/10, safety 6/10, novelty 4/10 — verdict **revise**. The mechanism is the strongest possible for AGA - dutasteride is an established, efficacious AGA drug and local dual type I/II blockade is a coherent target (PMID 40110814 does support abnormal 5-alpha-reductase elevation as pathogenic). However, the load-bearing evidence claim is misrepresented: PMID 39954111 is a 45-patient trial (15/arm) in which the microneedling+minoxidil+finasteride arm was NOT significantly better than minoxidil+finasteride alone on hair density or shaft diameter (group C vs B: P>0.05 for both); the claimed significant superiority of adding microneedling 'over drugs alone' on hair-density measures is not what the abstract reports - significance appears only against minoxidil monotherapy and on Norwood-Hamilton grade/self-rating. So the trial at best weakly validates microneedling as an adjunct, and says nothing about dutasteride or about microneedling as a topical-delivery enhancer specifically. Novelty is also overstated: intradermal dutasteride (mesotherapy injections) and topical dutasteride have already been studied in AGA, so 'microneedle-facilitated local dual 5AR blockade' is an incremental repackaging of an existing delivery idea, not a new paradigm. Safety plan is responsible (serum DHT monitoring, infection precautions) but the hypothesis never addresses dutasteride's long half-life and teratogenicity handling burden if meaningful systemic absorption does occur. Proceed only after correcting the PMID 39954111 characterization and adding actual topical/microneedle dutasteride pharmacokinetic data.

### 7. pentoxifylline (H008)

- ChEMBL: CHEMBL628 | Elo 1516 | confidence 2/5 | route: topical | origin: generation (round 1)
- **Mechanism:** Pentoxifylline is a topical-deliverable nonselective phosphodiesterase inhibitor (MW ~278) with two complementary, androgen-axis-orthogonal actions on dermal papilla biology: it downregulates TGF-beta1 (an effect documented clinically in fibrotic disease), and androgen-inducible TGF-beta1 secreted by dermal papilla cells is a key catagen-promoting, epithelial-growth-suppressing signal in miniaturization (dossier section 6); and PDE inhibition raises intracellular cAMP in dermal papilla cells, a growth-supporting signal. The final form locks in the falsifiable gate the prior round promised, with pre-declared success and failure criteria: organ-cultured human scalp follicles treated across the topically achievable concentration range, with dermal papilla TGF-beta1 secretion and cAMP as primary readouts and hair-shaft elongation plus anagen duration as functional endpoints; the hypothesis proceeds only if a concentration exists that lowers papilla TGF-beta1 by a pre-specified margin AND lengthens shaft growth, and self-terminates if the TGF-beta1 effect size at tolerable concentrations is negligible - the size-of-effect question the reviewer flagged as unknown.
- **Evidence:** PMID 40110814, a general AGA pathogenesis review, remains the only cited source and is used strictly at its actual level: follicle miniaturization with microinflammation is the problem statement, and existing drugs respond poorly. It is stated plainly that there is zero hair-specific evidence for pentoxifylline - no follicle culture, no animal alopecia model - so the hypothesis is a mechanism-targeted proposal whose entire evidentiary weight sits in the gating experiment above. The dossier (section 6) supplies the target rationale: local anti-TGF-beta strategies are unexplored in approved-drug space, and pentoxifylline's partial, indirect TGF-beta suppression is precisely why the effect size must be measured before any clinical thought. (refs: PMID 40110814)
- **Safety:** Topical-only delivery (fixed in the prior round per the original review) keeps systemic PDE inhibition - GI upset, dizziness, hypotension - irrelevant to a cosmetic indication. Pentoxifylline's small molecular weight and the documented follicular penetration of the related methylxanthine caffeine support topical feasibility, but scalp permeation is measured in the same study program rather than assumed. The partial, indirect nature of its TGF-beta lowering avoids the fibrosis/immunity/cancer-surveillance hazards of direct systemic TGF-beta blockade. Local irritation is the main expected risk; suitable for both sexes since the mechanism is not anti-androgenic.
- **Novelty rationale:** What materially changed in final form: the one remaining reviewer objection - that the TGF-beta effect size achievable at tolerable scalp doses is unknown and pentoxifylline's suppression is partial and indirect - is converted into a quantitative kill criterion inside the gating experiment (pre-specified TGF-beta1 reduction margin plus functional shaft-elongation endpoint), so the hypothesis can no longer survive a weak signal by vagueness. No approved drug is used in AGA for TGF-beta-axis or papilla-cAMP modulation, so this dual, androgen-orthogonal mechanism remains unexploited in hair medicine; it is positioned as an adjunct to AR-directed therapy, not a monotherapy.

Reviews:
- plausibility 6/10, evidence 3/10, safety 6/10, novelty 7/10 — verdict **revise**. The most interesting mechanistic angle in this set: pentoxifylline genuinely does downregulate TGF-beta1 (documented in fibrotic disease) and androgen-inducible TGF-beta1 from dermal papilla is a legitimate catagen-promoting target per the dossier (section 6). Two serious weaknesses. First, there is zero hair-specific evidence — no follicle culture, no animal alopecia model, nothing; the evidence_summary cites only a general AGA review, so the TGF-beta effect size achievable at tolerable doses in scalp is unknown, and pentoxifylline's TGF-beta suppression is partial and indirect at best. Second, the proposal lists oral delivery, which is wrong for a cosmetic indication — chronic systemic PDE inhibition (GI upset, dizziness, hypotension) to treat hair loss is a hard sell, and the microcirculation rationale echoes the weakest part of the minoxidil story (the vascular theory of AGA is contested). Revise to a topical-only formulation with an explicit follicle-culture TGF-beta readout before any clinical thought.

### 8. lovastatin (H009)

- ChEMBL: CHEMBL503 | Elo 1516 | confidence 2/5 | route: topical | origin: generation (round 1)
- **Mechanism:** Lovastatin is an HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor. Final form executes the reviewer's salvage condition exactly: the anti-androgen/steroidogenesis-substrate rationale is DROPPED, because statins' anti-androgenic signal in PCOS is a systemic gonadal/adrenal effect a topical scalp product cannot reproduce, and there is no established evidence the follicle synthesizes androgens de novo at a magnitude that matters. What remains is the local mevalonate-pathway arm: HMG-CoA reductase inhibition in scalp skin reduces isoprenoid intermediates required for protein prenylation (Rho/Rac/Ras family), a pleiotropic anti-inflammatory and pro-homeostatic action relevant to the perifollicular micro-inflammation documented in AGA (dossier section 9). Because prior topical-statin attempts in alopecia (mostly areata) were unimpressive, the hypothesis is gated rather than asserted: follicle-culture measurement of (a) prenylation-dependent inflammatory signaling under topical-achievable lovastatin concentrations and (b) - included specifically to close the dropped question empirically - follicular steroidogenic enzyme expression/androgen output, so the substrate rationale is refuted with data rather than merely abandoned. Proceeds only if a measurable local anti-inflammatory effect exists at tolerable exposure; positioned, if so, as an adjunct, not a monotherapy.
- **Evidence:** PMID 40110814 remains the only cited source and is used at its verified level: it associates microinflammation and metabolic-syndrome links with AGA pathogenesis and confirms the inadequacy of current drugs - it does not support any statin-in-follicle claim, and none is made. All mechanistic weight sits in the two-part follicle-culture gate; the reviewer's judgment that the androgen-substrate story targets a pathway that may not exist in scalp is accepted and converted into a measured sub-question rather than argued. (refs: PMID 40110814)
- **Safety:** Oral-statin liabilities (myopathy, liver-enzyme elevation) are irrelevant at topical exposure; systemic absorption from scalp application is expected to be negligible but is quantified in a first PK step. Pregnancy category X status is retained as a hard constraint: excluded from women who are or may become pregnant, which narrows but does not eliminate the cosmetic market. Local irritation is the main expected topical risk.
- **Novelty rationale:** What materially changed in final form: the hypothesis is rebuilt on the reviewer's terms - the core mechanistic leap (local anti-androgen via steroidogenesis substrate) is deleted as instructed, the defensible anti-inflammatory/mevalonate arm becomes the whole mechanism, the discarded arm is retained only as an empirical sub-measurement so its refutation is data-backed, and the unimpressive prior topical-statin alopecia attempts are conceded up front with confidence set accordingly. Local HMG-CoA reductase/prenylation modulation of perifollicular micro-inflammation has not been pursued in AGA with approved drugs; the value proposition is a cheap, safe, androgen-sparing adjunct candidate whose first experiment decides whether it exists at all.

Reviews:
- plausibility 4/10, evidence 3/10, safety 7/10, novelty 6/10 — verdict **revise**. The weakest link is the core mechanistic leap. Statins' anti-androgenic signal in PCOS is a modest systemic effect — reduced ovarian/adrenal steroidogenesis from lowered cholesterol substrate at the gonad. There is no established evidence that the hair follicle synthesizes androgens de novo at a level that matters in AGA; the disease is driven by follicular sensitivity to circulating DHT, and a topical statin cannot touch testicular/adrenal output. So the 'local steroidogenesis-substrate' story targets a pathway that may not exist at pharmacologically relevant magnitude in scalp. The anti-inflammatory arm (dossier section 9 microinflammation) is more defensible but nonspecific, and prior topical-statin-for-alopecia attempts (mostly alopecia areata) were unimpressive. Pregnancy category X also complicates a cosmetic product. Salvageable only if reframed around anti-inflammatory/HMG-CoA-reductase-local effects with direct follicular steroidogenesis measurements first — the androgen-substrate rationale as stated should be dropped.

### 9. spironolactone (H010)

- ChEMBL: CHEMBL1393 | Elo 1516 | confidence 3/5 | route: topical | origin: generation (round 1)
- **Mechanism:** Spironolactone is an androgen-receptor antagonist that also inhibits androgen biosynthesis; oral spironolactone is already used off-label for female-pattern hair loss. The final form sharpens the vague 'topical anti-androgen for men' premise into a specific, measurable target-engagement claim: topical spironolactone (or its active metabolite canrenone, which has prior topical formulation precedent) achieves follicular AR occupancy sufficient to suppress androgen-responsive signaling in dermal papilla cells at cosmetically acceptable doses with negligible systemic exposure. AR signaling in dermal papilla cells is the causal driver of miniaturization (dossier section 1), so a positive target-engagement readout has direct therapeutic meaning. The gating experiment is now concrete: ex vivo balding-scalp follicles and in vivo scalp skin treated with the topical formulation, read out by suppression of DHT-induced dermal papilla senescence markers and an androgen-responsive transcript signature in plucked follicles, alongside serum spironolactone/canrenone quantification.
- **Evidence:** PMID 39306884 validates AR-level blockade (preventing AR dimerization/nuclear translocation) as sufficient to rescue dermal papilla cells from DHT damage in vitro and in a DHT-induced mouse alopecia model - cited, as before, at the strategy level, since it tests obacunone, not spironolactone. PMID 24244503 shows AR signaling is required for androgen-induced dermal papilla senescence. The reviewer's accept verdict confirms this is mechanistically on-target evidence rather than by-association; the reviewer's residual point - that follicular AR occupancy at cosmetic doses is undemonstrated - is adopted as the hypothesis's defining measurement rather than rebutted. (refs: PMID 39306884, PMID 24244503)
- **Safety:** Oral spironolactone causes hyperkalemia, menstrual irregularities, and feminization in men - hence topical-only positioning with serum parent-and-metabolite quantification as a required study output. The reviewer's feminizing-exposure concern for women of childbearing potential is resolved by population sequencing: initial development targets men and women not of childbearing potential, with reproductive-population use gated on demonstrated negligible systemic levels. Local irritation is the main expected topical risk; hyperkalemia is implausible at topical exposure but is bounded by the same serum measurements.
- **Novelty rationale:** What materially changed in final form: (1) the reviewer's central undemonstrated link - follicular AR occupancy at cosmetic doses - is promoted from caveat to the hypothesis's explicit, measurable claim with named readouts; (2) the competitive-landscape caveat is made structural rather than rhetorical: with pyrilutamide/GT20029-era topical AR programs crowding the class, spironolactone is repositioned as the low-cost generic entrant whose differentiation is a published target-engagement dataset (follicle transcript signature plus serum levels), not novelty of mechanism; (3) the population-restriction plan converts the feminization risk from an open safety worry into a development-sequencing decision. No discovery novelty is claimed; topical spironolactone is an underexploited reformulation with the cheapest path to a rigorous occupancy readout in the class.

Reviews:
- plausibility 8/10, evidence 6/10, safety 7/10, novelty 4/10 — verdict **accept**. The strongest hypothesis in the set because it sits directly on the most validated axis in AGA: AR signaling in dermal papilla is causal, oral spironolactone already works off-label in female-pattern hair loss, and the cited support (PMID 39306884 showing AR-level blockade rescues dermal papilla from DHT damage in vitro and in a mouse model; PMID 24244503 on AR-dependent papilla senescence) is mechanistically on-target rather than by-association. The honest weakness is novelty, which the proposal itself flags: topical spironolactone (and its metabolite canrenone) has formulation precedent, patents, and small prior studies — this is an underexploited reformulation, not a discovery, and topical AR blockade as a class is already crowded by pyrilutamide/GT20029-era programs. Residual risks: feminizing exposure in women of childbearing potential even at low systemic levels, and whether topical spironolactone achieves follicular AR occupancy at cosmetically acceptable doses remains undemonstrated. Proceed, with the competitive-landscape caveat explicit.

### 10. finasteride (H011)

- ChEMBL: CHEMBL710 | Elo 1516 | confidence 3/5 | route: topical | origin: generation (round 1)
- **Mechanism:** Finasteride inhibits type II 5-alpha-reductase, lowering scalp DHT and relieving AR-driven dermal papilla dysfunction. The new angle is delivery, not mechanism: microneedling-assisted or otherwise physically enhanced transfollicular delivery of finasteride (e.g., topical finasteride combined with scalp microneedling) to achieve follicular 5-alpha-reductase inhibition with minimal systemic DHT suppression, addressing the non-response and sexual side-effect concerns of oral dosing.
- **Evidence:** PMID 39954111 shows that adding microneedling to 5% minoxidil plus finasteride significantly improved hair density and miniaturization metrics over minoxidil+finasteride alone in men with AGA, demonstrating that physically enhanced scalp delivery adds real clinical value to androgen-axis therapy. PMID 40110814 confirms finasteride's established role and that some patients respond poorly, motivating delivery optimization. (refs: PMID 39954111, PMID 40110814)
- **Safety:** Oral finasteride's sexual, mood, and (rare) post-finasteride concerns are dose/systemic-exposure related; topical-plus-microneedling delivery aims to retain follicular efficacy while lowering serum DHT suppression. Microneedling itself is low-risk (transient erythema, pinpoint bleeding) when performed with sterile technique. Topical finasteride must still be kept away from pregnant women due to teratogenic risk to a male fetus.
- **Novelty rationale:** Explicitly a new-angle re-proposal of an established drug: the mechanism is standard of care, but microneedling-enhanced topical delivery to decouple follicular efficacy from systemic exposure is a distinct, clinically grounded formulation hypothesis rather than a reworded copy.

Reviews:
- plausibility 7/10, evidence 5/10, safety 7/10, novelty 4/10 — verdict **revise**. The mechanism is not the hypothesis — finasteride's 5AR-II inhibition is standard of care — so this lives or dies on the delivery claim, and that claim is confounded. PMID 39954111 tests microneedling added to minoxidil PLUS finasteride; the incremental benefit of microneedling is equally (arguably more) consistent with wound-healing-induced growth stimulation and enhanced minoxidil uptake, not specifically with enhanced follicular delivery of finasteride. Attributing the gain to 'transfollicular finasteride delivery' is an unproven interpretation of a combination trial. Worse, the safety rationale is partly self-defeating: microneedling deliberately disrupts the stratum corneum, which increases systemic absorption of whatever is applied — the hypothesized decoupling of follicular efficacy from serum DHT suppression needs direct pharmacokinetic proof (serum DHT levels under microneedling-assisted topical dosing), not assumption. Novelty is also thin: topical finasteride is already an approved product in the EU, and microneedling-plus-topical combination protocols are widespread in the AGA literature. Salvageable if reframed honestly as a PK/pharmacodynamic question (does microneedling-assisted topical finasteride achieve follicular 5AR inhibition at lower serum DHT suppression than oral?) with a concrete measurement plan, and with the minoxidil confound addressed.

### 11. DIAZOXIDE (H027)

- ChEMBL: CHEMBL181 | Elo 1516 | confidence 3/5 | route: topical | origin: generation (round 3)
- **Mechanism:** Diazoxide is a direct ATP-sensitive potassium (KATP) channel opener that, unlike minoxidil, is pharmacologically active as administered and requires no bioactivation. Minoxidil is a prodrug whose follicular conversion to minoxidil sulfate by sulfotransferase SULT1A1 is variable between patients and is proposed to explain the large non-responder fraction (dossier section 5). A topically delivered, non-prodrug KATP opener would deliver channel opening to dermal papilla and follicular epithelium independent of each patient's follicular sulfotransferase activity, plausibly prolonging anagen through the same downstream mechanism as minoxidil sulfate while flattening response variability.
- **Evidence:** The strongest asset is the classic repurposing signal the dossier (section 11) calls proven: hypertrichosis is a well-documented adverse effect of systemic diazoxide in chronic use, i.e., this drug is already known to grow human hair when given systemically. Class-level clinical efficacy of follicular KATP opening in AGA is supported by the minoxidil arms of PMID 39954111. PMID 40110814 documents that a substantial fraction of patients respond poorly to the two approved drugs, which is the exact gap a SULT1A1-independent opener addresses. Honest gap shared with the rejected nicorandil proposal: the follicular KATP channel subtype (SUR1- vs SUR2-containing) is uncharacterized, and diazoxide opens both SUR1- and SUR2-containing channels, which partially mitigates but does not eliminate the subtype-matching risk. (refs: PMID 39954111, PMID 40110814)
- **Safety:** Systemic diazoxide causes hypotension, reflex tachycardia, sodium retention, and hyperglycemia (it inhibits insulin release) - oral use for a cosmetic indication is out of the question. The proposal is topical-only: diazoxide is a small molecule (MW ~231) with reasonable lipophilicity, a far better passive skin-penetration profile than minoxidil sulfate. Required gating experiment: percutaneous absorption study demonstrating negligible systemic exposure (no blood-pressure or glucose signal) at follicle-active scalp concentrations. Hypertrichosis at adjacent skin sites is a cosmetic risk to monitor, paradoxically also the on-target effect.
- **Novelty rationale:** Not an established hair treatment. It is differentiated from minoxidil by being a non-prodrug (removing the SULT1A1 responder-variability problem) and from the rejected nicorandil hypothesis (H003) by possessing the actual human hypertrichosis signal that nicorandil lacks, and by lacking nicorandil's nitrate-moiety tachyphylaxis. The dossier (section 5) explicitly names diazoxide as the approved-pharmacopeia KATP opener worth considering if topically viable.

Reviews:
- plausibility 8/10, evidence 6/10, safety 7/10, novelty 5/10 — verdict **accept**. Strongest of the set. It stacks the dossier's most reliable discovery signal (systemic diazoxide hypertrichosis is a real, reproducible human phenotype) on a class mechanism already clinically validated in AGA by minoxidil, and removes the SULT1A1 responder-variability problem by being a non-prodrug. Two reservations. First, the PMID 39954111 citation is mildly overreached: it is a small (n=45) minoxidil/finasteride/microneedling trial that says nothing about KATP channels — it supports minoxidil's clinical efficacy, not 'follicular KATP opening' as such; the KATP link is class inference from minoxidil pharmacology and should be stated that way. Second, the uncharacterized follicular KATP subtype is acknowledged but matters less than the nicorandil case because diazoxide's SUR1/SUR2 promiscuity covers both. Remaining real risks: pancreatic SUR1 engagement (hyperglycemia) if percutaneous absorption is non-trivial, and off-target hypertrichosis at adjacent skin. The required percutaneous-absorption gate is the right next step.

### 12. TACROLIMUS (H028)

- ChEMBL: CHEMBL3989887 | Elo 1516 | confidence 3/5 | route: topical | origin: generation (round 3)
- **Mechanism:** Tacrolimus (FK506) inhibits calcineurin, blocking NFAT dephosphorylation and nuclear translocation. The dossier (section 11) states that cyclosporine's hypertrichosis in transplant patients validates calcineurin/NFAT-adjacent pathways as hair-relevant, and NFATc1 activity in hair follicle stem cells is associated with stem-cell quiescence, so calcineurin inhibition plausibly promotes stem-cell activation and anagen entry. The proposal's core is delivery, not pathway discovery: tacrolimus is the one calcineurin inhibitor already approved as a topical dermatologic (atopic dermatitis ointment) with characterized low systemic absorption, directly solving the delivery problem that makes cyclosporine unusable for AGA.
- **Evidence:** Pathway validation is indirect but human and strong at the class level: systemic cyclosporine reliably causes hypertrichosis (dossier section 11). No provided excerpt tests tacrolimus on follicles, and this is stated plainly rather than laundered: the only citable excerpt, PMID 40110814, supports the AGA unmet-need framing only. The differentiating evidence is pharmacokinetic rather than biological: topical tacrolimus is an approved, marketed cutaneous product with quantified low systemic exposure, whereas cyclosporine (MW ~1202) penetrates skin poorly and the incumbent H012 (cyclosporine) was criticized for resting entirely on the systemic-observation-plus-generic-citation combination. (refs: PMID 40110814)
- **Safety:** Topical tacrolimus has a large dermatology safety base: main effects are transient burning/pruritus at the application site; systemic absorption through intact skin is minimal and trough levels are usually undetectable. A boxed malignancy warning exists for topical calcineurin inhibitors (lymphoma, skin cancer) based on theoretical and post-marketing signals - it must be addressed honestly for chronic cosmetic use on sun-exposed scalp, including UV-protection counseling. Not for use in pregnancy without risk-benefit review. No anti-androgenic or cardiovascular liability.
- **Novelty rationale:** Flagged proximity: incumbent H012 proposes cyclosporine on the same calcineurin/NFAT pathway and received a 'revise' verdict centered on systemic toxicity and thin delivery realism. Tacrolimus is proposed as the delivery-realistic member of the same validated class - a genuinely different drug with an approved topical formulation and quantified cutaneous pharmacokinetics, not a reworded copy. Tacrolimus itself has no established AGA indication, so the repositioning angle (right drug of the right class for a scalp product) is the novel contribution.

Reviews:
- plausibility 5/10, evidence 3/10, safety 8/10, novelty 4/10 — verdict **revise**. The delivery argument is the only genuinely new content and it is real — an approved topical calcineurin inhibitor with quantified low systemic exposure. But the biological case rests on class extrapolation from cyclosporine hypertrichosis, and cyclosporine's hair effect is not cleanly attributable to calcineurin/NFAT (CsA hits multiple targets including ATP-binding cassette transporters and has direct follicle effects tacrolimus may not share). The most damaging observation the hypothesis does not confront: topical tacrolimus ointment has been used on skin for over two decades in atopic dermatitis, and local hypertrichosis is at most a sporadic case-report phenomenon — if cutaneous calcineurin inhibition reliably grew hair, dermatology would have noticed. That real-world null undercuts the central extrapolation. Evidence is a single generic AGA review (PMID 40110814) used for unmet-need framing only. Salvageable only with a direct follicle organ-culture or mouse anagen-induction readout before any further commitment; otherwise this is H012 in better packaging.
